Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 43 would clarify that any local special tax on the ballot needs support from two-thirds of voters, rather than a simple majority. If passed, it would go into effect on Jan. 1.
Local taxes proposed by governments that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. But in recent years, California courts have allowed special taxes proposed by citizens to be approved with a simple majority vote, meaning more than half.
At the same time, the special interests pushing a tax hike are in some cases aligned with politicians on the measure, blurring the line between who is behind a proposed tax increase.

Backers argue that Proposition 43 is needed to close a loophole that makes it easier for groups, including business entities and unions, to seek special taxes.
Opponents contend that raising the threshold will make it harder to pass taxes and a lack of revenue will hurt communities seeking to fix roads or pay for public safety.

Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., Family Business Assn. of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability all back the measure. They want to rein in the ability of politicians and special interests to seek higher taxes and argue the cost of living in California is already too high.
Susan Shelley, vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn., argued in a Cal Matters opinion piece (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) that passage of Proposition 43 would clarify existing law.
Advertisement
“There is no ‘citizens’ initiative tax increase exception’ from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up,” she wrote. “Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes.”
One such case is Measure ULA, passed by L.A. voters in 2022. It created a tax on high-value real estate transactions to fund homeless initiatives. The measure passed with 58% of the vote, but opponents argued the two-thirds threshold should have been applied.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers, the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and the California School Employees Assn. all oppose the measure. They argue that it will make it harder to pass tax hikes to pay for police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts.
They also argue that Proposition 43 skirts the California Supreme Court’s opinion on the threshold.
Gubnatorial candidate Xavier Becerra opposes Proposition 43. In a statement, he called corporations “special interests” that want the proposition to pass in order to block new taxes.
Advertisement
“Prop. 43 would hand special interests the power to block the resources our communities count on most: fire protection, safe roads, good schools,” Becerrra said (https://www.noprop43ca.com/news/becerra-announces-opposition-to-proposition-43?source=ec60b1e8-1500-4301-8b7f-6c6ebde9cedd).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), who authored the legislation that became Proposition 43 — ACA 22 — opposes the measure and has urged Californians to vote against it. She said the only reason she crafted the bill was because it was a necessary bargaining chip to torpedo another ballot measure backed by the Jarvis taxpayers group that would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The fight over California tax policy has its roots in Proposition 13 (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-road-map-proposition-13-baby-boomers-20170709-story.html), the successful 1978 initiative that said local governments couldn’t increase taxes for specific purposes, such as road or school repairs, without the approval of two-thirds of local voters.
California voters also clarified that those taxes included assessments and other fees when they passed Proposition 218 in 1996.
In recent years, private groups seeking to raise local taxes have used voter-backed initiative petitions to get their measures on the ballot.
Advertisement
The California Supreme Court in 2017 indicated that the two-thirds threshold for local taxes applies to measures put on the ballot by elected government bodies, not to those sponsored by citizens.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 43 would clarify that any local special tax on the ballot needs support from two-thirds of voters, rather than a simple majority. If passed, it would go into effect on Jan. 1.
Local taxes proposed by governments that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. But in recent years, California courts have allowed special taxes proposed by citizens to be approved with a simple majority vote, meaning more than half.
At the same time, the special interests pushing a tax hike are in some cases aligned with politicians on the measure, blurring the line between who is behind a proposed tax increase.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., Family Business Assn. of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability all back the measure. They want to rein in the ability of politicians and special interests to seek higher taxes and argue the cost of living in California is already too high.
Susan Shelley, vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn., argued in a Cal Matters opinion piece (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) that passage of Proposition 43 would clarify existing law.

“There is no ‘citizens’ initiative tax increase exception’ from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up,” she wrote. “Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes.”
One such case is Measure ULA, passed by L.A. voters in 2022. It created a tax on high-value real estate transactions to fund homeless initiatives. The measure passed with 58% of the vote, but opponents argued the two-thirds threshold should have been applied.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers, the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and the California School Employees Assn. all oppose the measure. They argue that it will make it harder to pass tax hikes to pay for police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts.
They also argue that Proposition 43 skirts the California Supreme Court’s opinion on the threshold.
Gubnatorial candidate Xavier Becerra opposes Proposition 43. In a statement, he called corporations “special interests” that want the proposition to pass in order to block new taxes.

“Prop. 43 would hand special interests the power to block the resources our communities count on most: fire protection, safe roads, good schools,” Becerrra said (https://www.noprop43ca.com/news/becerra-announces-opposition-to-proposition-43?source=ec60b1e8-1500-4301-8b7f-6c6ebde9cedd).

California voters also clarified that those taxes included assessments and other fees when they passed Proposition 218 in 1996.
In recent years, private groups seeking to raise local taxes have used voter-backed initiative petitions to get their measures on the ballot.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?

43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-

Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.

ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30

measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.

A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 43 would clarify that any local special tax on the ballot needs support from two-thirds of voters, rather than a simple majority. If passed, it would go into effect on Jan. 1.
Local taxes proposed by governments that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. But in recent years, California courts have allowed special taxes proposed by citizens to be approved with a simple majority vote, meaning more than half.
At the same time, the special interests pushing a tax hike are in some cases aligned with politicians on the measure, blurring the line between who is behind a proposed tax increase.

Assembly Constitutional Amendment
No. 22
CHAPTER 132
A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A thereof, relating to taxation.
[
Filed with
Secretary of State
June 25, 2026.
]
LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
ACA 22, Wicks.
Local taxes: limitation.
The California Constitution conditions the imposition of a special tax by a local government upon the approval of 2 / 3 of the voters of the local government voting on that tax, and prohibits these entities from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property or a transactions or sales tax on the sale of real property.
The Supreme Court of California interpreted this provision and other provisions restricting the authority of local governments to impose, extend, or increase taxes as not restricting the authority of voters to impose taxes via initiative.
This measure would, beginning January 1, 2027, prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the
initiative power, from imposing, extending, or increasing any special tax, except as provided, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a 2 / 3 vote. The measure would prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided pursuant to specified constitutional provisions.

Bill Text
Resolved by the Assembly, the Senate concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2025–26 Regular Session commencing on the second day of December 2024, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California, that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:
That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIII A thereof, to read:
SEC. 4.5.
(a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided
in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.
(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIII C.

ACA22:v97#DOCUMENT Bill Start
Assembly Constitutional Amendment
No. 22
CHAPTER 132
A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A thereof, relating to taxation.
[
Filed with
Secretary of State
June 25, 2026.
]
LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
ACA 22, Wicks.
Local taxes: limitation.
The California Constitution conditions the imposition of a special tax by a local government upon the approval of 2 / 3 of the voters of the local government voting on that tax, and prohibits these entities from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property or a transactions or sales tax on the sale of real property.
The Supreme Court of California interpreted this provision and other provisions restricting the authority of local governments to impose, extend, or increase taxes as not restricting the authority of voters to impose taxes via initiative.
This measure would, beginning January 1, 2027, prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the
initiative power, from imposing, extending, or increasing any special tax, except as provided, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a 2 / 3 vote. The measure would prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided pursuant to specified constitutional provisions.
Digest Key
Vote:
2/3
Appropriation:
NO
Fiscal Committee:
NO
Local Program:
NO
Bill Text
Resolved by the Assembly, the Senate concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2025–26 Regular Session commencing on the second day of December 2024, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California, that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:
That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIII A thereof, to read:
SEC. 4.5.
(a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided
in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.
(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIII C.

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects
***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.

Proposition 43’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials.
If Prop.
43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop.
43 on the ballot since 2017 when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass.
The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling.
This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.

Assembly Constitutional Amendment

CHAPTER 132
A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A thereof, relating to taxation.
[
Filed with
Secretary of State
June 25, 2026.

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
ACA 22, Wicks.
Local taxes: limitation.
The California Constitution conditions the imposition of a special tax by a local government upon the approval of 2 / 3 of the voters of the local government voting on that tax, and prohibits these entities from imposing an ad valorem tax on real property or a transactions or sales tax on the sale of real property.
The Supreme Court of California interpreted this provision and other provisions restricting the authority of local governments to impose, extend, or increase taxes as not restricting the authority of voters to impose taxes via initiative.
This measure would, beginning January 1, 2027, prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the
initiative power, from imposing, extending, or increasing any special tax, except as provided, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a 2 / 3 vote. The measure would prohibit a local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided pursuant to specified constitutional provisions.

Resolved by the Assembly, the Senate concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2025–26 Regular Session commencing on the second day of December 2024, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California, that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:
That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIII A thereof, to read:
SEC. 4.5.
(a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided
in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.

### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.

Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes.

Proposition 43’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes.
Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials.
If Prop.
43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.

California’s Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State’s History of Local Tax Limits
Aravind Boddupalli
Display Date
October 27, 2026
Next month, California voters will decide whether to require a two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes, or taxes dedicated to a specific purpose.
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would reverse a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) that have allowed these measures to pass with a simple majority, raising their approval threshold to the same one that local lawmakers face to enact these taxes. If passed, it would apply to measures placed on ballots on or after January 1, 2027.
While cities, counties, and special districts provide essential services, including fire protection, roads, parks, and libraries, their ability to raise taxes is governed by a complicated set of statewide rules. Proposition 43 could further constrain local governments’ ability to raise revenue, even for services supported by a majority of voters.
California’s fiscal history and comparisons with other states offer some perspective on what the change could mean for local governments and the communities they serve.
California's fiscal rules are nearly 50 years in the making
Proposition 43 joins a lineage of statewide measures (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2669) that reshaped local public finances starting in the late 1970s. A few notable examples:
Proposition 13 (1978) capped property tax rates and required two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, which later came to be defined as taxes dedicated to special purposes.
Proposition 218 (1996) added restrictions on local governments' ability to raise revenue, including new simple majority voter-approval requirements for new general taxes and property-related fees.
Proposition 39 (2000) lowered the voter threshold for qualifying school facility bonds from two-thirds to 55 percent, moving in the opposite direction.
Proposition 26 (2010) broadened the definition of taxes subject to voter approval.
The result is a complicated set of institutional rules where revenue changes face different voter-approval requirements depending on their type, how revenue will be used, and whether voters or legislators placed the proposal on the ballot.
California is not the only state revisiting supermajority requirements in November. Voters in South Dakota and Utah (https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=21126) will consider measures that would require higher approval thresholds for certain tax or constitutional changes. But California's debate is different: It centers on voter-initiated local tax measures rather than statewide tax initiatives or statewide constitutional amendments.
The California Budget and Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/) identifies several recent voter-initiated special taxes that passed with a simple majority vote. Examples include San Francisco’s tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, and Fresno’s increase of its local sales tax rate to fund community parks.
What the revenue patterns reveal
According to TPC’s analysis of the 2024 Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (https://state-local-finance-data.taxpolicycenter.org/pages.cfm), California ranked 37 th among states on the share of local general revenue coming from own-source revenues, like taxes, fees, or charges, rather than federal or state government transfers (Figure 1).
Since 1977, just before Proposition 13 began reshaping California's local finances, growth in local own-source revenue has trailed growth in state own-source revenue, although some of this reflects different tax bases at each government level, including the state's reliance on income taxes and local governments' heavier reliance on property taxes and fees (Figure 2).
Together, these figures suggest that California's local governments remain somewhat reliant on state decisions and intergovernmental funding streams. However, local governments continue to deliver many public services. This disconnect can weaken efficiency and accountability, as noted (https://lao.ca.gov/analysis_1993/MGMS_reprint_02-93.html) by the state's Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
And, if Proposition 43 makes it more challenging for local governments to raise revenues, local lawmakers may need to increase general taxes, reduce government spending, or look to state lawmakers to help foot their bills. Unlike special taxes, general taxes are not earmarked to be spent for a particular purpose. Voters who support a tax that specifically pays for child care or community parks may be less willing to support a general tax that goes into a government's general fund and could be spent across a wide range of activities.
Further, localities within California differ substantially in wealth, economic opportunity, and fiscal capacity. Jurisdictions with stronger property tax bases and local economies can often generate more revenue from the same available tax policy than communities with fewer resources (https://www.gfoa.org/materials/addressing-resource-inequities). If dedicated local revenues from special taxes are harder to secure, those disparities in fiscal capacity and maintenance of services between poorer and wealthy jurisdictions could widen, raising potential equity (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/state-and-local-government-revenues-and-racial-disparities) concerns (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/more-than-fines-and-fees-incorporating-equity-city-revenue-strategies).
California has seen before how voting rules affect tax measures
Prior research (https://www.ppic.org/publication/fiscal-effects-of-voter-approval-requirements-on-local-governments/) found that voter approval rates vary considerably by type of revenue measure, with transportation, fire protection, and education-related measures receiving the most support.
And after Proposition 39 lowered the approval threshold for school facility bond measures in 2000, passage rates increased by nearly 30 percent, according to the LAO (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2978), even though average share of voters supporting the measures remained roughly flat.
California’s voting rules create a contradiction
Voters often prefer taxes dedicated to a specific purpose (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/ReformVoteSwap.pdf), yet California generally requires higher approval thresholds for those taxes than for general taxes.
Proposition 43 would extend the two-thirds approval requirement, which currently applies to local lawmakers, to voters who propose local special taxes. Supporters could argue that requiring broader agreement protects taxpayers from increases that lack widespread support. But the higher threshold would also make it harder to pass tax measures that a majority of voters do support.
California’s history suggests that voter-approval thresholds matter. The question facing voters in November is whether requiring broader support for local special taxes is worth potentially limiting communities’ ability to raise revenue for public services.

Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.

What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. However, local voters’ ability to propose new special taxes to protect or strengthen key services would be limited as local voter initiatives would become much more challenging to pass. Additionally, voters in special districts would face a higher bar to increase revenues to preserve and expand services, regardless of whether the funds would be targeted to specific programs.
Proposition 43’s Constraints on Local Revenues Would Make Things Harder for Communities Already Struggling
Governments across the board have felt the impacts of inflation on the costs of providing public services, and the state’s aging population increasing the cost of providing some services such as health care. The impacts of the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law, (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) H.R. 1 — also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — along with the effects of climate change, the labor market (https://immresearch.org/reports/ice-arrests-result-in-a-decline-in-employment-state-level-projections/) and broader economic impacts (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/Economic%20Impact%20of%20Mass%20Deportation_June%202025.pdf) of arrests and deportations of immigrants, and other federal policy changes such as tariffs, are also creating challenges for localities.

SUMMARY
Overall, voters were slightly more supportive of the
local bond and tax measures in the 2023 local
elections (73.3%) than the 2025 local elections
(63.0%). The number of measures requiring a
majority to pass jumped from 2 in 2023 to 11 in
2025, eight of which were for sales tax increases
primarily for General Government purposes and three
of which were special taxes placed on the ballot by
citizen initiative requiring only a simple majority for
passage instead of two-thirds. The 2023 elections
had one combined parcel tax and special tax bond
that did not pass whereas in 2025 there were two,
both of which passed. In 2023, Public Health and
Safety measures comprised 46.7% of all ballot
measures, however in the 2025 local elections,
measures proposed for that purpose dropped to
18.5%. Ballot measures for General Government and
Capital Improvements and Public Works purposes
totaled 7 tax measures each or 25.9% of the 2025
total. In both elections, the passage rate for the
region of Los Angeles remained at 100%. The
passage rate of special tax measures was lower in
2025 (47.1%), then in 2023 (76.0%).

The two-thirds vote requirement for taxes is fair
August 10, 2026
Share Page
Proposition 43, appearing on this November’s statewide ballot, will close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13 that gave the green light to local governments to impose local special taxes without the two-thirds vote required by the plain language of Prop. 13.
Section 4 of Prop. 13 states, in unambiguous terms, that special taxes may only be approved “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” Nonetheless, the courts have ruled that the two-thirds vote requirement would not apply if the tax was placed on the ballot by a “citizens’ initiative.”
These more recent decisions are in direct conflict with an earlier ruling in Altadena Library District v. Bloodgood, decided in 1987. There the California Court of Appeal relied on the plain language of Prop. 13 finding that the two-thirds (2/3) supermajority voter approval requirement for local “special taxes” mandated by Section 4 applies fully to citizens’ ballot initiatives, as well as taxes proposed by local governing boards.
Because Proposition 43 restores the original 2/3 voter threshold for special taxes, it was inevitable that the tax and spend interests would, once again, argue that supermajority vote requirements are somehow inherently undemocratic. Although this contention has been repeatedly discredited, it is helpful to understand why supermajority votes are critical to any functioning government.
First, higher voting thresholds protect minority interests by inhibiting the targeting of specific, smaller groups or industries with high taxes. By ensuring a broader consensus, it requires lawmakers (or voters) to build wide agreement across party lines before taking more private income for public use. Supermajorities also help to stabilize tax policy by making it harder to change frequently, which creates a more predictable economic environment for taxpayers and businesses.
Second, supermajority vote requirements also foster fiscal discipline by forcing lawmakers to prioritize existing funds and cut waste instead of reflexively raising taxes to cover deficits. They also encourage governments to find efficient, structural solutions for budget problems rather than relying on new revenue.
Third, higher voter thresholds enhance democratic legitimacy by ensuring that major fiscal changes represent a large percentage of the population, not just a bare 51% majority. Decisions made with a supermajority carry higher public acceptance and compliance.
Finally, supermajority vote thresholds are nothing new and have a long history in America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation has a long history dating back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
At both the state and federal levels, our constitutional framework is replete with checks and balances which, in theory, constrain the ability of government to deprive us of life, liberty and property. And there is no more draconian power of government than the power to tax. As this nation’s first Chief Justice, John Marshall, noted in 1819, “The power to tax is the power to destroy.”
Jon Coupal is president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)

Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.

Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
